name: QGIS
purpose: Full desktop geographic information system for viewing, editing, analysing and publishing spatial data, with hundreds of processing algorithms and a large plugin ecosystem.
journalism_use_case: The workbench for any story with a spatial claim: overlay satellite imagery against a conflict incident's coordinates, measure distances and areas from imagery for damage assessment, join a leaked contracts dataset to administrative boundaries, or georeference a scanned historical map to compare land use over decades.
pros: The only tool here that lets a non-programmer do serious spatial analysis — georeferencing, measurement, raster algebra, buffer and overlay operations — which is the difference between a mapped story and a guessed one
Georeferencing scanned maps and imagery is a distinctive investigative capability: it turns a photographed or leaked map into something you can measure against satellite data
Enormous plugin ecosystem including satellite-imagery loaders, OSM downloaders and Sentinel Hub integration, so acquisition and analysis happen in one place
Actively maintained under OSGeo governance with a long-term-release track (final-3_44_15, 2026-09-25) and daily commits
cons: Steep learning curve and a dense interface: a reporter will need training, and a bad projection choice silently produces wrong distances and areas — the most common and most consequential mistake
5,500 open issues (the largest in the catalogue), reflecting both scale and a long accumulated backlog; expect to encounter rough edges in less-used algorithms
Heavy desktop application, awkward on low-powered machines and unsuitable for scripted pipelines (use GDAL/geopandas for that)
GPL-2.0 means plugin and derivative distribution carries copyleft obligations — immaterial for internal analysis, relevant if you ship a tool
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 14,853 stars with 5,500 open issues, release final-3_44_15 (2026-09-25), pushed 2026-11-17, GPL-2.0. QGIS is the standard open GIS in both the geospatial and data-journalism communities, reflected in its adoption across OSGeo and in journalism training curricula.
assessment: Adopt it as the newsroom's spatial workbench and invest in training one or two analysts properly — the capability-per-trained-analyst is very high, and spatial claims are where investigations get challenged. For your profile the single most valuable discipline to impose is projection hygiene: record the CRS used for every measurement, because an area calculated in Web Mercator at high latitude can be wrong by a factor that would embarrass a published story.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release final-3_44_15 (2026-09-25), 14,853 stars, 5,500 open issues. Daily commits, structured long-term-release and point-release cadence, OSGeo institutional governance with a funded development model. The vast issue count reflects two decades of accumulation at scale, not neglect.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Data layers you load (satellite imagery, OSM extracts, commercial basemaps) carry their own licences, which is where the real restrictions sit.
licence_restrictions: GPL-2.0 on the application; plugins distributed for QGIS generally inherit copyleft expectations. The practical licence risk in GIS work is the DATA — commercial satellite imagery and some national mapping data forbid redistribution of derived products, so check before publishing a map.
costs: No software fee. Runs on an analyst workstation; large raster work wants plenty of RAM and SSD. The costs that bite are data: commercial satellite imagery and tasking are priced per scene or per km² by the vendor (not priced here; see Sentinel Hub/Planet entry). Analyst training time is the other real cost.
privacy: Fully local analysis — imagery and datasets stay on your machine. Two things to watch: plugins may call external services, and loading a basemap from a commercial tile provider sends your viewport (hence your area of interest) to that provider. For a sensitive location, use local imagery rather than a live basemap.
alternatives: geopandas plus rasterio for scripted, reproducible analysis
GDAL for command-line raster and vector conversion
kepler.gl or QGIS2Web for publishing rather than analysing
summary: Full desktop geographic information system for viewing, editing, analysing and publishing spatial data…

name: GDAL
purpose: Translator library and command-line suite for raster and vector geospatial formats, with reprojection, warping, mosaicking, clipping and format conversion across several hundred drivers.
journalism_use_case: The plumbing under every spatial pipeline: convert a government shapefile to GeoJSON for the web, reproject a leaked dataset into a measurable coordinate system, clip a 40GB satellite scene to the area of interest, or mosaic tiles into a single image for before-and-after comparison.
pros: Format coverage no alternative matches, including the awkward national and legacy formats that government data arrives in — the practical reason it is unavoidable
Command-line tools (gdalwarp, gdal_translate, ogr2ogr) make reprojection and clipping scriptable and reproducible, which is what a defensible methodology needs
Underpins QGIS, geopandas, rasterio and most of the geospatial ecosystem, so learning it pays off across every other tool
Very actively maintained (v3.13.3, 2026-08-18; pushed 2026-11-17) under OSGeo with a professional release process
cons: Licensing is an aggregate: the LICENSE.TXT read in this survey is a collection of licences covering the tree (MIT-licensed core plus many component licences), so a redistribution review means reading the file rather than trusting a single SPDX label — GitHub reports NOASSERTION for exactly this reason
Command-line ergonomics are notoriously unfriendly: flag semantics are inconsistent across tools and error messages are cryptic
603 open issues and a very large driver surface, so obscure format bugs are a real possibility
Easy to produce silently wrong output — a reprojection with a wrong source CRS assumption looks fine and is not
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 6,159 stars with 603 open issues, release v3.13.3 (2026-08-18), pushed 2026-11-17, SPDX NOASSERTION with an aggregate LICENSE.TXT (read and saved in this session's evidence). Its position as the foundation of the geospatial ecosystem is verifiable from the dependency declarations of QGIS, rasterio and geopandas.
assessment: Adopt — you will use it whether you choose to or not, since it sits beneath everything else. For your profile the practical advice is to standardise a small set of scripted GDAL invocations (reproject, clip, convert) with explicit CRS arguments and keep them in version control, rather than running ad-hoc commands; that makes spatial preprocessing reproducible. Read LICENSE.TXT once if you ever intend to redistribute a GDAL-bundled product, because the aggregate licensing genuinely requires it.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v3.13.3 (2026-08-18), 6,159 stars, 603 open issues. Regular versioned releases under OSGeo governance with corporate contributors and a security process.
licence: Aggregate — LICENSE.TXT (read 2026-11-17) collects the licences applying across the tree: an MIT-licensed core plus many component licences. GitHub reports NOASSERTION
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Data you process carries its own licence.
licence_restrictions: Core is MIT-style, but the aggregate file exists because components differ — some drivers depend on libraries with stricter terms. For internal use this is immaterial; for redistributing a bundled binary, read LICENSE.TXT and check which drivers you ship.
costs: No fee. CPU and disk proportional to imagery size — clipping a large scene is I/O-bound. Negligible licensing cost; infrastructure estimate only.
privacy: Local processing with no network calls unless you point it at a remote dataset (GDAL can read over HTTP/S3, in which case the host sees your range requests and therefore your area of interest).
alternatives: rasterio and geopandas for Pythonic access to the same underlying capability
QGIS for interactive rather than scripted work
DuckDB spatial for SQL-based vector analysis
summary: Translator library and command-line suite for raster and vector geospatial formats, with reprojection, warping, mosaicking…

name: geopandas
purpose: Python library extending pandas with geometry columns, providing spatial joins, overlays, buffering, dissolving, reprojection and plotting over vector data.
journalism_use_case: The scripted counterpart to QGIS for reproducible spatial analysis: join a leaked list of addresses to electoral boundaries to show which districts a scheme benefited, count incidents within a radius of military installations, or dissolve parcel data by owner to reveal concentrated land holdings.
pros: Reproducibility is the decisive advantage over desktop GIS: a notebook documenting every spatial operation can be rerun, reviewed and published as methodology, which a sequence of QGIS clicks cannot
Familiar pandas idioms mean a data journalist already comfortable with dataframes can do spatial joins without learning GIS software
BSD-3-Clause with active maintenance (v1.2.0, 2026-09-28) and a 1.x stable API after a long pre-1.0 period
Integrates with the whole Python data stack, so spatial results flow directly into charts, tables and further analysis
cons: Spatial joins on large datasets are memory-hungry and slow compared with a spatial database — above a few million geometries you want PostGIS or DuckDB spatial
437 open issues and a dependency chain (shapely, pyproj, GDAL bindings) that is a frequent source of installation pain, especially on Windows

Reprojection correctness is the user's responsibility: geopandas will happily compute a wrong area if you forget to project out of degrees, and it is the single most common error in published spatial journalism
No visualisation beyond basic matplotlib plots, so publication-quality maps need another tool
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,301 stars with 437 open issues, release v1.2.0 (2026-09-28), pushed 2026-11-14, BSD-3-Clause. Widely used in data journalism, reflected in its prominence in the field's teaching materials.
assessment: Adopt as the default for any spatial analysis that will inform a published claim, precisely because the notebook is the methodology. For your profile I would pair it with one habit: assert the CRS explicitly at the top of every analysis and compute areas and distances only in a projected CRS appropriate to the region. That single discipline prevents the most common category of spatial error in journalism.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v1.2.0 (2026-09-28), 5,301 stars, 437 open issues. Regular releases on a stable 1.x line with a broad contributor base and NumFOCUS-adjacent governance.
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Datasets carry their own licences.
costs: No fee. CPU and RAM proportional to dataset size; memory is the binding constraint on large joins. Negligible infrastructure for typical newsroom datasets.
privacy: Local processing. Note that some convenience functions can download basemaps or example datasets from external hosts — review before use on an isolated machine.
alternatives: DuckDB spatial or PostGIS for datasets too large for memory
QGIS for interactive exploration and georeferencing
rasterio for raster rather than vector analysis
summary: Python library extending pandas with geometry columns, providing spatial joins, overlays, buffering, dissolving…

name: rasterio
purpose: Pythonic interface to GDAL's raster capabilities, reading and writing geospatial raster datasets as NumPy arrays with windowed reads, reprojection and masking.
journalism_use_case: The analysis layer for satellite work: compute a vegetation or burn index to show deforestation or fire damage over time, difference two scenes to detect new construction at a military or industrial site, or extract pixel values at incident coordinates to corroborate a claim about ground conditions.
pros: Windowed reads let you work with a small area of a very large scene without loading it all, which is what makes satellite analysis practical on an ordinary machine
NumPy array interface means band arithmetic (NDVI, NBR, change detection) is a few lines, so the analytical techniques used in environmental and conflict reporting are directly accessible
BSD-3-Clause (licence read in this session — GitHub reports NOASSERTION) with active maintenance (1.5.2, 2026-09-30)
Clean, well-documented Pythonic API that avoids GDAL's command-line awkwardness while using the same engine
cons: Depends on GDAL, so installation inherits that complexity — wheels have improved this but environment conflicts remain the common complaint
Raster analysis is easy to do wrong: cloud masking, scaling factors and band-specific preprocessing all materially affect an index, and an uncorrected result can show change that is not there
158 open issues and release-tag hygiene is mixed (latest tag 'rtd-deps-tag' alongside the 1.5.2 release), so pinning needs care
No visualisation or georeferencing UI — analysis only
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 2,595 stars with 158 open issues, release 1.5.2 (2026-09-30), pushed 2026-11-03, licence resolved to BSD-3-Clause by reading LICENSE.txt (Mapbox copyright) since GitHub reports NOASSERTION.
assessment: Adopt for satellite analysis, with a methodological caution that matters more than the tooling: before publishing a change-detection finding, verify that the apparent change is not an artefact of cloud cover, seasonal variation, sensor differences or scaling. For your profile the strongest pattern is to pair rasterio analysis with manual visual confirmation in QGIS on the same scenes — the index tells you where to look, the human confirms what is there.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-03, latest release 1.5.2 (2026-09-30), 2,595 stars, 158 open issues. Regular releases with a broad contributor base; two weeks since last push is normal cadence for a mature library.
licence: BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE.txt read 2026-11-17, Mapbox copyright; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Satellite imagery carries the provider's licence — this is where restrictions actually apply.
licence_restrictions: Code permissive. The material restrictions are on imagery: Sentinel and Landsat are openly licensed, but commercial providers (Planet, Maxar) restrict redistribution of imagery and sometimes of derived products — check before publishing a processed image.
costs: No fee. CPU and disk proportional to scene size; satellite scenes are large (hundreds of MB to GB each). The real cost is imagery acquisition where commercial data is needed. Estimate.
privacy: Local processing. If reading remotely (S3, HTTP), the host sees your range requests and therefore your area of interest — relevant when the area itself is sensitive.
alternatives: GDAL command-line tools for one-off conversion and clipping
QGIS for visual analysis and georeferencing
sentinelhub-py or pystac for acquiring the imagery in the first place
summary: Pythonic interface to GDAL's raster capabilities, reading and writing geospatial raster datasets as NumPy arrays with windowed…

name: Overpass API
purpose: Database engine and query language for OpenStreetMap data, allowing selection of map features by tag, area, proximity and time, served via public instances or self-hosted.
journalism_use_case: The engine behind feature-based geolocation and infrastructure mapping: find every petrol station within 2km of a coordinate to match a photographed sign, enumerate all military installations tagged in a region, or extract every school in a district to cross-reference against a procurement dataset.
pros: Tag-and-proximity querying is the core technique of feature-based geolocation — 'find places with a church, a water tower and a railway within 500m' is exactly how photographs get located
Historical (attic) data support lets you query what OSM said at a past date, which is useful for establishing what existed when
AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable, so a newsroom can run its own instance and keep queries private — a genuine advantage since queries reveal your area of interest
Underpins overpass-turbo, overpy, OSMPythonTools and bellingcat/osm-search, so the whole OSM investigative toolchain rests on it
cons: Self-hosting is a serious undertaking: a full planet instance needs substantial disk and hours of import time, and most users therefore rely on public instances
Public instances see your queries, which disclose precisely which locations and feature combinations you are investigating — a real operational-security consideration
Query language is idiosyncratic and unforgiving; learning it takes real effort and errors often return empty results rather than diagnostics
Slowing cadence: last push 2026-02-19 with the latest release osm3s_v0.7.62.4 from 2024-11-21, and 224 open issues
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 945 stars with 224 open issues, release osm3s_v0.7.62.4 (2024-11-21), last push 2026-02-19, AGPL-3.0. Its central position in OSM tooling is verifiable from the dependency relationships of overpass-turbo, overpy and bellingcat/osm-search.
assessment: Essential capability, and for your profile the question is where you run it. Public instances are free and convenient but disclose your geolocation targets; a self-hosted regional extract (not the full planet) is a realistic middle path that keeps queries private and is far cheaper than a global instance. Given the slowing release cadence, note it as a dependency to watch — the public instances' continuity matters more to you than the repository's.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-02-19, latest release osm3s_v0.7.62.4 (2024-11-21), 945 stars, 224 open issues. Nine months without commits and two years since the last release, on infrastructure the whole OSM query ecosystem depends on. Declining rather than dormant; no deprecation notice and the public instances remain operational.
model_or_data_licence: OpenStreetMap data is ODbL 1.0 — a share-alike database licence with attribution and, for derived databases, share-alike obligations.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0 on the engine. More importantly, ODbL on the DATA: publishing a derived database (not merely a map image) obliges you to license it under ODbL and attribute OSM. This catches newsrooms that publish extracted datasets without realising.
costs: No fee. Public instances are free but rate-limited. Self-hosting estimate: a regional extract is feasible on one VM with a few hundred GB of disk; a full planet instance needs terabyte-class storage and a long import. Assumptions: self-hosted regional extract.
privacy: Queries to a public instance disclose your area of interest and the feature combinations you are matching — which in a geolocation investigation is close to disclosing the case. Self-hosting eliminates this and is the reason to consider it.
alternatives: bellingcat/osm-search for a journalist-friendly proximity-search interface over the same data
overpass-turbo for interactive query development
Downloading a regional OSM extract and querying it locally with PostGIS or DuckDB spatial
blockers: Public-instance queries disclose geolocation targets; self-hosting is required for private querying
summary: Database engine and query language for OpenStreetMap data, allowing selection of map features by tag, area, proximity and time…

name: overpass-turbo
purpose: Web-based interactive development environment for Overpass API queries, with a map view, query wizard, syntax highlighting and result export to GeoJSON, GPX and KML.
journalism_use_case: The practical way to develop a feature-based geolocation query: use the wizard to build 'all water towers in this bounding box', see results on the map immediately, refine, then export the candidates as GeoJSON for comparison against the photograph.
pros: Interactive map feedback makes the Overpass query language learnable, which it is not from documentation alone — this is the tool that makes OSM querying accessible to a non-engineer
The query wizard translates plain descriptions into Overpass QL, lowering the barrier substantially for one-off investigative queries
Export to GeoJSON/KML means results flow straight into QGIS or a map for visual comparison
MIT licensed (resolved in this session — GitHub reports NOASSERTION) and still maintained (pushed 2026-10-25)
cons: Using the public overpass-turbo.eu instance sends your queries and bounding boxes to that service, disclosing exactly which locations you are investigating — the same exposure as public Overpass instances
No release objects at all (latest tag dated 2020-01-07) and 262 open issues against 1,269 stars, so versioning is informal and the backlog is substantial
Depends on the Overpass API, which is itself showing declining maintenance — a two-layer dependency risk
Browser-based with large result sets causing performance problems; it is a development tool rather than a batch interface
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,269 stars with 262 open issues, no releases, latest tag dated 2020-01-07, last push 2026-10-25; licence resolved to MIT by reading the blob, which also notes bundled libraries carry their own licences.
assessment: Adopt for query development, then move the finished query to a private path for the actual work — that two-step is the privacy-preserving pattern. For your profile: develop interactively on the public instance using an innocuous nearby area, then run the real query against your own Overpass instance or a local extract so the genuine coordinates never reach a third party. The tool's value is pedagogical and exploratory, and it is excellent at that.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-10-25, no release objects, latest tag dated 2020-01-07, SPDX NOASSERTION (MIT per the licence blob), 1,269 stars, 262 open issues. Commits within the last month but no release engineering since 2020; a widely used tool maintained at minimal velocity.
licence: MIT (licence blob read 2026-11-17, which notes bundled libraries have their own licences; GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
licence_restrictions: MIT on the application. ODbL obligations attach to exported OSM data if you publish a derived database.
costs: No fee. The public instance is free and rate-limited; self-hosting the front end is a static deployment.
privacy: Queries on the public instance are visible to that service and to the Overpass instance behind it, disclosing your area of interest. Self-host the front end and point it at your own Overpass instance for private work.
alternatives: bellingcat/osm-search for a purpose-built journalistic proximity search
python-overpy or OSMPythonTools for scripted querying
A local OSM extract in PostGIS for fully private querying
blockers: Public instance discloses queries and bounding boxes
summary: Web-based interactive development environment for Overpass API queries, with a map view, query wizard…

name: python-overpy
purpose: Python wrapper for the Overpass API that submits queries and parses the response into typed node, way and relation objects.
journalism_use_case: Scripted, repeatable OSM queries inside an investigation pipeline — for example iterating a list of 200 claimed incident coordinates and extracting the nearby tagged features for each, which is impractical by hand in overpass-turbo.
pros: Typed result objects remove the tedious JSON parsing that otherwise clutters OSM scripts
MIT licensed, small, and simple enough to read entirely — easy to audit and to replace if needed
Still maintained (pushed 2026-11-02), which is reassuring given that its upstream Overpass API has slowed
Works against any Overpass instance including your own, so the privacy decision is yours
cons: No release objects (latest tag 0.7), so pinning relies on tags or PyPI versions rather than release notes
Inherits Overpass API rate limits and availability, so batch work against a public instance will be throttled and should not be relied on for deadline work
Thin wrapper: it adds convenience, not capability, and you still need to write Overpass QL
Small community (266 stars, 29 open issues) with limited examples for investigative patterns
feedback: No individual user reports verified. Documented: 266 stars with 29 open issues, no releases, latest tag 0.7, last push 2026-11-02, MIT licence.
assessment: Integrate it for scripted OSM work, pointed at your own Overpass instance rather than a public one if the coordinates are sensitive. For your profile the batch pattern — iterate coordinates, extract nearby features, score candidate matches against what a photograph shows — is a genuinely strong semi-automated geolocation approach, and this library is the simplest way to build it. Plan around rate limits by running against a local extract.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-02, no releases, latest tag 0.7, 266 stars, 29 open issues. Recent commits on a small, feature-complete wrapper; low velocity is appropriate to its scope.
licence_restrictions: None on the code; ODbL obligations attach to published derived databases.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. Public Overpass instances are free but rate-limited; a local instance is the cost consideration.

alternatives: OSMPythonTools for a richer but GPL-3.0 and slower-moving alternative
Direct HTTP requests to Overpass, which is barely harder
OSMnx where the target is street networks rather than arbitrary features
summary: Python wrapper for the Overpass API that submits queries and parses the response into typed node, way and relation objects

name: OSMnx
purpose: Python library that downloads OpenStreetMap street networks and other geospatial features, builds them as NetworkX graphs, and provides routing, centrality, orientation and morphology analysis.
journalism_use_case: Analyse movement and access questions with a spatial basis: compute how long an ambulance journey actually takes from a neighbourhood to the nearest hospital, test whether a claimed route in a video is physically plausible in the available time, or measure how a new road or checkpoint changes accessibility for a community.
pros: Turns street data into an analysable graph, which lets you make quantitative accessibility claims — a strong, defensible basis for public-interest reporting on health, transport and segregation
Routing and travel-time analysis provides a physical-plausibility test for claims about movement in videos or testimony, which is a distinctive verification capability
MIT licensed, exceptionally maintained (pushed 2026-11-17, latest tag v2.1.2) with essentially no open issues (1) against 5,902 stars — the cleanest tracker in this segment
Excellent documentation with published academic methodology, so the analysis is citable
cons: Analysis quality depends entirely on OSM completeness, which varies enormously by region — in under-mapped areas the network is incomplete and travel-time results will be optimistic
No release objects on GitHub (tag v2.1.2 only), so pinning relies on tags or PyPI
Downloading large networks from Overpass is slow and rate-limited; city-scale is fine, country-scale needs a local extract
Routing uses simple impedance models, so results are a plausibility estimate rather than a traffic simulation — presenting them as actual travel times would overstate them
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,902 stars with 1 open issue and same-day commits (2026-11-17), MIT licence. The near-empty issue tracker at this scale is exceptional and the strongest maintenance evidence in this segment. The project has a published academic methodology, which is relevant credibility for citation.
assessment: Adopt for any story with an access, distance or movement claim — it gives you numbers you can defend, which is rare in spatial reporting. For your profile the two cautions are: check OSM completeness for your region before trusting travel-time results, and describe outputs as modelled rather than measured times. The plausibility-testing use (could someone have travelled that route in that time?) is an underused verification technique worth building into your workflow.

licence_restrictions: None on the code. ODbL attribution and share-alike apply if you publish a derived database of OSM features.
costs: No fee. CPU and RAM for graph analysis; city-scale networks are comfortable on a laptop. Downloading from public Overpass is free but rate-limited. Estimate.
privacy: Network downloads go to Overpass (public instance unless configured otherwise), disclosing the areas you are analysing. Analysis itself is local.
alternatives: Direct Overpass queries plus NetworkX if you want more control
QGIS network analysis tools for interactive work
Valhalla or OSRM for serious routing with realistic impedances

name: osm-search
purpose: Tool that searches OpenStreetMap for combinations of features in proximity to each other, returning candidate locations where the specified features all occur nearby.
journalism_use_case: The core feature-based geolocation workflow made usable: a photograph shows a church, a football pitch and a water tower, so you search for places where all three occur within a given radius and get a shortlist of candidate locations to check against satellite imagery.
pros: Implements exactly the technique practising geolocation investigators use, with an interface a non-engineer can operate — removing the Overpass QL barrier entirely
Proximity-combination search is the highest-leverage geolocation method available for photographs with identifiable landmarks, and this is the most accessible implementation of it
MIT licensed and built by Bellingcat, whose investigators use these methods daily
Self-hostable, so the queries (and hence the case) need not go to a third party
cons: Results depend entirely on OSM tagging completeness: a water tower that nobody mapped will not be found, and in under-mapped regions the method degrades sharply — which is where conflict reporting often is
Candidate lists still require manual verification against imagery, so it narrows rather than solves — and a confident shortlist can anchor an investigator on a wrong region
Small project (217 stars, 11 open issues) with no releases and last push 2026-07-07, so it is maintained at low velocity
Using the hosted version discloses the feature combination you are searching for, which is a meaningful hint about your case
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 217 stars with 11 open issues, no releases, last push 2026-07-07, MIT licence. The feature-proximity geolocation method it implements is extensively documented in Bellingcat's published investigations, which is strong contextual evidence that the technique works.
assessment: Adopt — and self-host it if geolocation work is routine for you, both for privacy and because the hosted instance is a dependency. For your profile the realistic expectation is that it works well in Europe and well-mapped regions and poorly where OSM coverage is thin; in those areas the fallback is manual satellite survey of plausible regions, informed by GeoCLIP. Always treat the shortlist as hypotheses and verify each against imagery before narrowing.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-07-07, no releases or tags, 217 stars, 11 open issues. Four months since last push on a small focused tool from an institutional maintainer; functionally complete rather than abandoned.
licence_restrictions: None on the code; ODbL obligations attach to published derived OSM datasets.
costs: No fee. Self-hosting needs an Overpass instance or access to one — the real infrastructure consideration. Estimate.
privacy: The hosted version discloses your searched feature combinations to the operator and to the Overpass instance behind it. Self-hosting with your own Overpass keeps the case private.
alternatives: overpass-turbo for hand-written equivalent queries
GeoCLIP to narrow the region before feature search
Manual satellite survey where OSM coverage is inadequate
